bib.title: Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search", Sahil Sen, Akhil Kasturi, Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Vamse Kumar Subbiah (PwC U.S.). arXiv:2605.15184v1 [cs.CL], 14 May 2026. Preprint, no venue. Path: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/02-context-engineering/sources/sen-2026-grep-all-you-need.pdf

COVERAGE: All 9 pages, 46,488 of 46,488 chars (body, Tables 1-4, Limitations, Conclusion, references, Appendix A). Figure 1 is an image. I read only its caption, not the plot.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: With inline tool delivery, grep beat vector on every one of the 10 harness-model pairs.
  number: Chronos + Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 86.2 vs 62.9 (largest gap); Claude Code + Opus 4.6 76.7 vs 75.0 (smallest)
  setup: 116-question LongMemEval-S subset, full haystack, inline delivery, GPT-4o grader, Chronos-preprocessed sessions. Five models, four harnesses (Chronos, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI). Single run per cell, no confidence intervals reported.
  quote: "inline grep exceeds inline vector for every harness–model pair. The largest margin is Chronos with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (86.2% vs. 62.9%), and the narrowest is Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.6 (76.7% vs. 75.0%)."
  where: p.4, section 4.1.3, Table 1 on p.5
- Claude's harness choice moves accuracy as much as the retriever does.
  number: Opus 4.6 gets 93.1% on Chronos but 76.7% on Claude Code, both inline grep.
  setup: same as above.
  quote: "The same Claude Opus 4.6 backbone reaches 93.1% under Chronos but 76.7% under Claude Code, so changing the harness shifts the ceiling by roughly as much as swapping retrievers within a fixed harness."
  where: p.4, 4.1.3
- Claim: On Chronos, inline grep spans a higher range than inline vector. Codex with GPT-5.4 ties the best Chronos grep.
  number: Chronos grep 83.6-93.1%, vector 62.9-83.6%. Codex GPT-5.4 grep 93.1 vs vector 75.9.
  setup: inline, full haystack.
  quote: "On Chronos, inline grep spans 83.6–93.1% across backbones, whereas inline vector spans 62.9–83.6%."
  where: p.4
- Claim: File-based (programmatic) delivery reshuffles the comparison. Vector beats grep on 5 of 10 pairs. Grep programmatic collapses on Codex.
  number: Codex GPT-5.4 grep falls from 93.1% (inline) to 55.2% (programmatic); programmatic vector is 67.2%.
  setup: same as above; the model must write results to a file, then read or search the file.
  quote: "The sharpest regression is Codex with GPT-5.4, which falls from 93.1% under inline grep to 55.2% under programmatic grep, with programmatic vector at 67.2% for that same pair."
  where: p.4, Table 1
- Claim: Weak model on a CLI harness does badly, and grep still leads.
  number: Haiku 4.5 on Claude Code: inline grep 55.2 vs vector 44.0; programmatic 37.1 vs 32.8.
  setup: as above. The paper's explanation is a hypothesis, with no trace-level analysis.
  quote: "Claude Haiku 4.5 on Claude Code (55.2% inline grep vs. 44.0% inline vector, and 37.1% vs. 32.8% programmatic)"
  where: p.4
- Claim: Table 1 in full (accuracy %, order: grep inline / vector inline / grep programmatic / vector programmatic).
  number: Opus Chronos 93.1/83.6/80.2/81.9; Opus Claude Code 76.7/75.0/68.1/79.3; Haiku Chronos 83.6/76.7/83.6/81.9; Haiku Claude Code 55.2/44.0/37.1/32.8; GPT-5.4 Chronos 89.7/81.9/87.1/75.0; GPT-5.4 Codex 93.1/75.9/55.2/67.2; Gemini 3.1 Pro Chronos 91.4/82.8/79.3/76.7; Gemini 3.1 Pro Gemini CLI 81.9/75.0/81.0/82.8; Flash-Lite Chronos 86.2/62.9/85.3/72.4; Flash-Lite Gemini CLI 87.1/67.2/68.1/74.1
  setup: as above.
  quote: "Claude Opus 4.6 Chronos 93.1 83.6 80.2 81.9"
  where: p.5, Table 1
- Claim: Noise scaling is not monotone, and neither retriever degrades smoothly. Vector often leads at small session limits. The crossover depends on harness and backbone.
  number: Chronos Opus grep 89.3/89.7/90.5/85.3/89.7 at s5/s10/s20/s30/full; vector 94.0/94.8/92.2/84.5/92.2. Claude Code Opus grep 91.4/94.0/95.7/90.5/94.0; vector 77.6/72.4/75.0/78.4/72.4. Gemini CLI Pro at full: vector 89.7 vs grep 78.5. Chronos Gemini 3.1 Pro at full: grep 86.6 vs vector 84.5.
  setup: Experiment 2. Same 116 questions. Session limit s5, s10, s20, s30 or full (39-66 sessions). Oracle sessions always kept; distractors filled from the same bundle and redrawn for each limit. Inline delivery. GPT-4o grader.
  quote: "Our scaling study partially supports this — vector retrieval is often stronger at low session counts — but reveals that the crossover depends on harness and backbone rather than corpus size alone."
  where: p.6, 4.2.3-4.2.4, Tables 2-3 on p.7
- Claim: Harness-specific preferences stay stable across the noise sweep.
  number: Claude Code favors grep for Opus and Haiku at every limit; Gemini CLI Pro favors vector at every limit.
  setup: Experiment 2.
  quote: "Claude Code favors grep for Opus and Haiku at every configuration we report, Gemini CLI Pro favors vector throughout"
  where: p.6
- Claim: Figure 1 shows both methods degrade little as noise is added, and grep is higher on average.
  number: none (plot only)
  setup: mean over the Experiment 2 grid.
  quote: "Mean performance as noise is added to the retrieval pool. Both methods face minimal degradation, but GREP outperforms vector on average."
  where: p.6, Fig. 1
- Claim: Per-category grep accuracy on Chronos (full haystack) varies widely. GPT-5.4 is weakest on temporal reasoning and multi-session.
  number: GPT-5.4 TR 67.7; MS 74.2. Opus MS 83.9. Single-session-assistant is 92.3-100 for all models.
  setup: Chronos, grep-only, full haystack, n=116. Categories: KU, MS, SS-A, SS-P, SS-U, TR. The appendix text says "inline", while the main text says "programmatic" (see PROBLEMS).
  quote: "GPT-5.4 77.8 74.2 92.3 85.7 93.8 67.7"
  where: p.9, Table 4
- Claim (author interpretation, untested): LongMemEval rewards literal spans, so lexical precision wins. Grep fails on vocabulary mismatch, and dense retrieval pulls in topical near-misses.
  number: none
  setup: hypothesis only. The paper does not isolate query strings or retrieved sets.
  quote: "Table 1 is consistent with a regime where LongMemEval’s answers are often licensed by a small set of literal spans, so the precision bias of lexical matching wins when hits are injected inline and immediately actionable."
  where: p.5
- Claim: File-based delivery trades context bandwidth for tool-use competence. It helps only if the agent reliably reads and integrates the file.
  number: none
  setup: interpretation of Table 1.
  quote: "programmatic routing trades context bandwidth for compositional tool competence; gains are realized only when the agent reliably closes the loop."
  where: p.5

LIMITS
- Authors concede: conclusions are tied to long-memory conversational QA with verbatim-heavy answers. They say "We do not claim that grep “beats” vector in general, only that it can win end-to-end under the task distribution and corpora we study." Dense or hybrid retrieval may differ on paraphrased, visual or code corpora (p.7).
- Incomplete grids: Codex vector scaling is complete only at full, and there is no Codex grep scaling row.
- Distractors are redrawn at each session limit, so mid-grid peaks are sampling noise ("stochastic outer loop", p.7).
- No trace-level causal attribution. Mechanisms are labelled hypotheses.
- Not shown: no hybrid (grep plus vector) condition, even though hybrid is listed as future work. No significance tests or seeds. n=116, so one question is about 0.86 points.
- Chronos preprocessing adds structured temporal events to both retrievers, which is not a plain-text corpus.
- The vector side uses a reranker and an agent-chosen top-k. The Chronos harness starts with top-15 vector results as an initial context block, which may favor vector in "grep-only" runs. The embedding model is not named.
- The grader is GPT-4o. Models are the 2026 versions (Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1).
- Authors are PwC and the harness (Chronos) is their own. Not peer reviewed.

BUILDS ON: LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025, ICLR) for benchmark and grader protocol; Chronos (Sen et al., 2026, arXiv:2603.16862) for the harness and temporal-event preprocessing; BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021); DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020); BM25 and weak-baseline critique (Lin, 2019); SPLADE v2 (Formal et al., 2021); ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020); RRF (Cormack et al., 2009); Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2024) for context rot; MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023); SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) for CLI harnesses; ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); Luan et al. (2021) for sparse-dense complementarity; Lumer et al. (2025) MemTool and tool-selection survey.

CODE: none. The paper has no code. The nearest thing is the description of the grep tool: regex over in-memory turns and events, "Results are scored by match count and returned" (p.3).

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p.6), mean performance versus added noise (session limit), grep versus vector. It summarizes Tables 2-3 in one view. I did not run the figures script. Only the caption was read.

PROBLEMS
- Internal inconsistencies for the caller to check before citing numbers:
  - Table 1 inline grep (full haystack) vs Table 2 "full" grep. Chronos Opus is 93.1 vs 89.7. Claude Code Opus is 76.7 vs 94.0. Claude Code Haiku is 55.2 vs 81.9. Gemini CLI Pro is 81.9 vs 78.5.
  - Table 1 vector vs Table 3 "full". Chronos Opus is 83.6 vs 92.2. Gemini CLI Pro is 75.0 vs 89.7.
  - The two tables are described as the same setting, and no reason for the differences is given.
  - Text says Chronos Opus vector at full is "92.2%". The text also says "Claude Code Opus is weakest at s10 (72.4%)", but Table 3 shows 72.4 at both s10 and full.
  - The text says that for Chronos Opus "grep is ahead at the penultimate limits: 85.3% vs. 84.5%", which matches s30 only.
  - The Section 4.1.3 pointer to Appendix Table 4 says "programmatic", but Appendix A says "inline".
  - The abstract says grep "generally" wins; the conclusion says "consistently", but the data show reversals.
- The extraction contains no embedded instructions. Figure 1 is not readable as text.
